findings: `phone` is declared `TEXT NULL` in schema.sql (line 14) but the `User` TypeScript interface declares `phone: string` as non-optional/non-null (User.ts line 24); `listActiveUsers()` returns raw query rows cast to `User[]` with no null-check or coalescing, so any row with `phone IS NULL` will silently violate the type contract and crash any downstream code that calls string methods on `user.phone`.

`signup()` performs a non-atomic check-then-insert for email uniqueness (SELECT at line 35, INSERT at lines 37-40) against a table with no UNIQUE constraint on email (explicitly noted at schema.sql line 16); two concurrent signup calls with the same email can both pass the SELECT check before either INSERT commits, producing duplicate email rows (TOCTOU race).

`listActiveUsers()` (line 30-32) selects from `users` with no `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` filter despite the table having a `deleted_at` column (schema.sql line 13) and the function being named 'active users' — it will return soft-deleted users as if they were active.

The email-uniqueness check in `signup()` (`WHERE email=$1`, line 35) is case-sensitive with no normalization (e.g. `LOWER(email)`), so 'user@example.com' and 'User@Example.com' are treated as distinct, allowing effectively duplicate accounts despite the intended uniqueness check.

The 'email taken' check in `signup()` does not exclude soft-deleted rows (`deleted_at IS NOT NULL`), so a previously deleted account's email permanently blocks re-signup with that same email, which is likely unintended given the soft-delete design.

The `User` interface has no `deleted_at` field at all, so nothing in the type system reflects or enforces the soft-delete semantics that the schema and `listActiveUsers` naming imply, making the active/deleted distinction invisible to consumers of `User`.
